newsitem.title: UK: HI-TECH, FINANCE, DRUG STOCKS SEEN AS SECTOR WINNERS.
newsitem.headline: HI-TECH, FINANCE, DRUG STOCKS SEEN AS SECTOR WINNERS.

text.p: The high technology, financial and pharmaceutical sectors, already strong performers in equity investment portfolios worldwide, are hot tips again for 1997, a Reuters poll of fund managers and analysts showed on Friday.

A worldwide survey of which equity sectors stand to gain and lose most during the coming year showed that fund managers were set, amid a broad-based range of dislikes, to show particular caution towards paper and pulp products and public utilities.

The poll was conducted between December 3 and 10. Fund managers and strategists based in Britain, the United States, Japan, Luxembourg, Switzerland and Germany were asked to give their forecasts for winning and losing sectors, both in their speciality spheres and globally during 1997. MARKET LOVE AFFAIR WITH COMPUTERS, HI-TECHS TO CONTINUE
The world's developing love affair with computers and high technology would ensure that sector remains a boom area, they said.

"Historically, we have always favoured high technology as a sector and that's not going to change in 1997," said Bob Bissell, senior vice-president at Wells Fargo Bank, giving particular mention to companies specialising in computer networking and storage.
Analysts saw the hi-tech sector spreading its net beyond the established giants of the business to envelop smaller firms.

"We expect the leadership among technology shares to broaden. A better economy will allow other technology companies to participate," said Steve Reynolds, chief investment officer for U.S. equities at Zurich Kemper Investments.
While the U.S. market saw the greatest hi-tech advances being made in software, Japanese equities analysts and fund managers expected their hardware sector to continue to boom.
Toyo Securities strategist Haruo Nakaharu said the strong high-tech sector would be supported by telecoms demand. ASIA, BRITAIN, GERMANY IN FAVOUR BUT U.S. NOT TIPPED
Geographically, Asia, Britain and Germany were seen to be in favour with fund managers, while the the United States was forecast to be feeling off-colour during 1997.

That reflects the findings of this week's Reuters survey of the 1997 outlook for the world's top 15 bourses, which saw a retreat of the U.S. Dow and Nasdaq indices from current levels but strong performances from Japan, Hong Kong and Taiwan.
In emerging markets, Brazil, Chile, India and Egypt were given honourable mention and South Korea was seen to be strongly undervalued.
But some fund managers expected a strong desire for the security of established markets to outweigh the risks of venturing into riskier areas of the developing world.

The ageing populations of Japan, the United States and Western Europe continue to put health care and the pharmaceuticals sectors in the spotlight, analysts said. PHARMACEUTICALS SEEN AS GOOD BET INTERNATIONALLY
Pharmaceuticals, after a rash of takeovers, would enjoy the benefits of rationalisation and synergy to make them a good bet internationally, analysts said.

"Quite simply, chemicals and drugs are very export-oriented companies and I expect a continuing stronger dollar. Despite their strong performance this year, I still expect these sectors to provide a very interesting investment alternative next year," said Walter Schmidt, head of fund management at Cologne-based Gerling Investment Kapitalanlegegesellschaft.

"One area we like in Europe, and in most parts of the world, would be drugs stocks," said Gavin Gemmell, a senior partner with Edinburgh-based Baillie Gifford, which has nearly 12 billion pounds ($20 billion) under investment.
"Some of the big Swiss companies have merged, so economies of scale and cost-cutting are a major feature."

"I like managed health care as a good performing sector. Drugs will be a good sector and I would add the multinational sector as a catch-all group," said John Cleland, chief investment strategist at U.S.-based Security Benefit Group.
Poor performers in the United States would include the sectors most affected by slowing economic growth, he said.
These include chemicals, steels and papers.
In Europe, cyclicals were seen to expect a better following in 1997 as economies picked up strength.

"There is so much good potential and visibility now in European corporate restructuring," said Marc Polydor, investment manager of Swiss private bank Union Bancaire Privee. "In Europe earnings will rise. There will be a lot of investment opportunities." BRITISH ECONOMIC RECOVERY SEEN BOOSTING CONSUMER SECTOR
Britain's economic recovery bodes well for the consumer sector, analysts said.

"The easy call is to be in the consumer retailing sector. Particularly if a Labour government is in place, people might be keener on the building and construction sector," said Gary Dugan, European equity market strategist with JP Morgan.

David Binnie, fund manager at Scottish Life, was bearish about alcohol firms and British utilities. "These companies will produce below-average earnings growth...In alcohol firms, there is a combination of micro and macro factors. We are not terribly impressed with the quality of management," he said.
Many analysts said that selecting sectors was becoming a risky venture and the onus was on fund managers to pinpoint particular companies.

"In Europe sector rotation is less important than it was a few years ago -- it is more to do with individual companies. People expect them to adapt to world conditions and some do, while some don't," said Roland Werdel, portfolio manager at Credit Suisse in Luxembourg. ($1=.6043 Pound)
